splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines or criminal statutes.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should apply the rule of lenity or defer to the Sentencing Commission's interpretation when a Guidelines provision is ambiguous in a criminal context. This matters because it determines whether ambiguity in sentencing rules is resolved in favor of the defendant or the government's preferred reading.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, so ambiguity must be resolved in the defendant's favor.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes priority over the rule of lenity, allowing courts to defer to the Commission's anti-defendant interpretation of ambiguous Guidelines provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1's expansion of the guideline text.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders under the Guidelines.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and controls
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the Guidelines entitled to deference, so inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the plain text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, making Application Note 1 an impermissible expansion rather than an interpretation, and thus not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), operates conjunctively (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctively (any single criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether a defendant must meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any one criterion is sufficient. The split directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses and creates geographic disparities in criminal sentencing.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria are satisfied.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' effectively means 'or,' so possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state statute covers a substance not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be controlled under federal law or whether state-law controlled substances suffice. This affects career-offender and enhanced base offense level determinations for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State schedule suffices
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law, with no requirement that the substance also be federally scheduled.

positions.label: Federal schedule required
positions.summary: Holds that a prior conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's amendments to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) stacking) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in the law, alone or combined with other factors, can support a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. This affects thousands of federal prisoners serving sentences that would be lower under current law.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot contribute
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may contribute
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive sentencing changes can be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly in combination with other factors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must challenge conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions (such as denial of earned time credits) exclusively through habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or whether civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens) are also available.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement that affect the duration of imprisonment, or whether civil rights claims can also be brought. This affects federal prisoners seeking to challenge BOP decisions on First Step Act earned time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-affecting claims
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's claim effectively challenges the fact or duration of confinement, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy, precluding civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may pursue civil rights claims to challenge conditions of confinement even when those conditions may affect the duration of imprisonment, and habeas is not the exclusive remedy.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether property appreciation occurring between the initial Chapter 13 filing and the conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the estate or the debtor. This matters significantly for debtors whose homes appreciate during a Chapter 13 case, as it determines whether a trustee can sell the home to pay creditors after conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and § 541(a), post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, not to the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) was enacted to protect good-faith converting debtors, and post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor rather than the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly consider punishment as a purpose when revoking supervised release and imposing a sentence, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to the sanctioning purposes listed in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether punishment is a permissible purpose at supervised release revocation sentencing. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts expressly to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, while other circuits hold that the statutory purposes of revocation sentencing do not include punishment. This affects hundreds of revocation proceedings each year.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose punishment when sentencing a defendant upon revocation of supervised release.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that the purposes of revocation sentencing under § 3583(e) do not include punishment, and courts must focus on the statutory factors rather than punitive objectives.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil deadline (30 days) or the criminal deadline (14 days) under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of the appellate filing deadline. The majority view treats it as civil (30-day deadline), but a minority applies the criminal deadline. This affects defendants' ability to timely appeal denials of attorney's fees in criminal cases.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion arises from the criminal case and is therefore subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on the timing requirement for actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA. The question is whether assumptions must be locked in by the end of the plan year or whether actuaries retain discretion to select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined as of the statutory measurement date and cannot be selected or changed afterward.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary retains discretion to select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require assumptions to be fixed by year-end.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, extending the court's jurisdiction to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to extend the term beyond what was specified in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — when bringing successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners are barred from raising any previously presented claim; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the gatekeeping bar of § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring previously raised claims in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy the separate requirements of § 2255(h).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The split affects whether election administration rules can be challenged before elections take place, with significant implications for mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when a state law changes the rules governing how votes are counted, even before the election occurs.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's speculative and generalized injury from a ballot-counting rule is insufficient for Article III standing without a concrete showing of competitive harm.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as an order that is 'effectively unreviewable on appeal from final judgment.'
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether orders denying motions to seal documents containing private medical information qualify for immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine. The D.C. Circuit holds they do because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' while other circuits have applied stricter standards limiting collateral order review of sealing decisions.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because maintaining medical privacy is a value of high order that would be irreparably lost if review were delayed.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are generally not immediately appealable because the privacy interest, while significant, does not meet the stringent requirements of the collateral order doctrine.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal questions regarding fair treatment standards, discrimination liability, and damages in the hospitality and service industries. The grant suggests a circuit split on the applicable legal framework for such claims.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied standards for discrimination claims in hospitality establishments that the Supreme Court found sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a distinctive approach to liability and remedies.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the disagreement that prompted Supreme Court review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
